cards.back: During a network partition, a replicated system must choose between consistency (every read sees the latest write or errors) and availability (every request gets a non-error answer). Partitions always happen, so 'CA' is not a real option.

If Partitioned, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose Latency or Consistency. Waiting for remote replicas costs tens to hundreds of milliseconds even on a healthy network, so the latency trade is the one you usually feel.

ACID (atomic, consistent, isolated, durable) is what a relational database promises for a transaction. BASE (basically available, soft state, eventually consistent) is the AP side of CAP as a design stance; most systems mix both.
A reader sees the latest committed write, as if there were one copy. Use it for balances, inventory, unique usernames, leader election and locks.
A user always sees at least their own latest writes. Typical for profile edits and seeing a comment right after posting it.
A reader never sees an older value after a newer one. It prevents 'the comment appeared, then vanished on refresh'.
Effects appear after their causes, such as a reply after the message it replies to. Used in chat, comment threads and collaborative apps.
With N replicas, a write waits for W confirmations and a read asks R replicas. If R + W > N, every read set overlaps every write set in at least one replica, so reads see the latest successful write.
Read repair fixes a stale replica noticed during a quorum read, hinted handoff replays writes held for a down node, and anti-entropy compares replicas in the background with Merkle trees.

Last write wins by timestamp is simple but silently drops a write and trusts drifting clocks. Alternatives are version numbers with compare-and-set, keeping both versions for the app to merge, or CRDTs.
A sequence of local transactions across services, each with a compensating action if a later step fails, such as releasing stock when the card charge fails. Pair it with the outbox pattern.

quiz.q: N = 3, W = 2, R = 2. Which is true?
choices: Reads overlap the latest write and the system survives one replica down
Reads may miss the latest write
Any single replica failure blocks writes
It needs a leader to be consistent
quiz.why: 2 + 2 > 3, and two of three replicas can still form both quorums.

quiz.q: For seat booking, what consistency choice does the page recommend?
choices: CP for the seat, AP for the seat map
CP for everything, including the map
Eventual for the seat, strong for the map
quiz.why: Only the final reservation must be exact; the map can be slightly stale.

quiz.q: Why is 'CA' not a real choice for a distributed system?
choices: Network partitions happen in any real network
Consistency and availability are the same thing
CA systems cannot use replicas at all
CA only works with leaderless stores
quiz.why: CAP forces the choice during a partition, and partitions cannot be ruled out.

quiz.q: A user posts a comment, refreshes, and it vanishes, then reappears. Which guarantee is missing?
quiz.why: Monotonic reads guarantee you never see an older value after a newer one.

quiz.q: What is the main problem with last-write-wins conflict resolution?
choices: It silently drops one of the writes and depends on clocks that drift
quiz.why: The losing write disappears without anyone being told.

quiz.q: Two services each own a database. How do you keep a multi-step order consistent?
choices: One distributed ACID transaction across both
quiz.why: Separate databases cannot share one transaction, so each step gets an undo.

quiz.q: In DynamoDB, what does a strongly consistent read cost compared with an eventual read?
quiz.why: The page's real-world table notes strongly consistent reads use twice the read capacity.
